title: The Kolkata Value Hunters Club; Q&A with Mohnish Pabrai
summary: Pabrai explains how reading about Nick Sleep in 'Richer, Wiser, Happier' shifted him toward holding great compounders indefinitely with a promoter's mindset, illustrated by scaled-economies-shared businesses like Costco and Amazon, his Turkish warehouse investment, Rain Industries, and Naspers' 8,000x on Tencent. He also covers Indian Hotels' poor capital allocation, 'funeral' businesses, Covid-era bottom-up investing, his empty-calendar daily routine, and the origins and scale of Dakshana.

ideas.idea: Nick Sleep and Qais Zakaria showed that a handful of great businesses held with almost no activity can beat nearly every fund manager.
ideas.detail: Nomad managed about $3 billion in 2014 with Amazon near a third of capital; under regulator pressure they returned capital, each with roughly $100 million, and Nick put everything into Amazon, Costco and Berkshire while Zak spread across six stocks and never traded since. Amazon went from about $300 to $3,300 a share. The Nomad letters are freely available online and chapter six of 'Richer, Wiser, Happier' is worth reading.

ideas.idea: Growth and value are two sides of the same coin: every business is worth its discounted lifetime cash flows, so a rapidly growing stream deserves a higher price.
ideas.detail: Buying Amazon does not make it a non-value stock and buying a company at one-fifth of book does not make it a great value stock. He admits he shifted to a Grahamian approach before the dotcom bubble, was up about 70% a year in 1999-2000 with no losses, but 'forgot to switch back' to his original preference for high-ROE growth businesses.

ideas.idea: Scaled economies shared, where a business gives the benefits of scale back to customers, produces very long runways and is one of the most powerful business models.
ideas.detail: MasterCard keeps the spoils of its 20-25 basis point take rate, but Costco caps markups at 15% versus 25-30% at Walmart or Amazon, treats itself as a buying agent for members, and earns essentially only the membership fee; its wine buyers guarantee vineyards 20 years of output at fair prices. Each new Costco makes all Costcos stronger; Amazon and Berkshire's insurance follow the same track.

ideas.idea: D-Mart succeeds because its model blends Costco and Walmart, which is why nobody in India can touch it.
ideas.detail: He says Avenue Supermarts took many lessons from Costco, and counts D-Mart among good businesses alongside MasterCard, Costco and Berkshire.

ideas.idea: Ask the Walmart question: if you owned a great compounder in 1980 or 1990, what would make you sell, and if you owned K-Mart, what would make you keep it?
ideas.detail: Walmart has been public 51 years and only the Walton family has held it the whole time, collecting dividends through three generations. Nick Sleep's insight is that answering those two questions well is the core of long-term investing.

ideas.idea: Think of yourself as the promoter, or the junior partner of the promoter, of a business rather than as an investor, and hold as long as the trajectory keeps improving.
ideas.detail: Indian promoters commonly own 50-70% of listed businesses and keep their wealth concentrated there because they know the business best. His new model is not to sell at 90-100% of intrinsic value but to keep owning for 10, 20 or 30 years while the business gets better.

ideas.idea: In 2019 he bought one-third of Turkey's largest warehouse, truck and rail operator for $7 million at a $19 million market cap against $300 million to $1 billion of liquidation value.
ideas.detail: The company traded at roughly 2-7% of liquidation value with 12 million square feet of fully leased warehouses; his only question was whether the promoters were crooks. Turkey is one of the best markets because local investors have extremely short holding periods, expecting to buy at 10am and sell at noon for 10%.

ideas.idea: The key question for a great business is its destination: what will it look like in 10 or 20 years and with what probability?
ideas.detail: Capitalism is so brutal that most businesses cannot be forecast that far, but some, like Costco, give comfort; Costco's first China store had mile-long lines and could have 1,000 stores in 20 years, so a shareholder need make no decisions and just hold.

ideas.idea: Rain Industries was a no-lose deep-value bet that went 10x, but it is a good business with a great capital allocator, not the great business a Nick Sleep framework would target.
ideas.detail: In 2015 he bought the 9.99% foreign-investor maximum at 35-40 rupees when Jagan Reddy had grown revenue from $200 million to $2 billion through two non-recourse, fully debt-financed acquisitions (a US business for $600-650 million and Rutgers in Europe for $900 million) that the market valued at zero. Earnings hit $200 million in 2017-18, the stock went to 450, fell to 50 in Covid, and sits around 170-180; he still holds because Reddy spends about $10 million a year extra on pollution control and thinks long term.

ideas.idea: India is a minefield where the truly great businesses generally trade at very elevated valuations, with only occasional dislocations.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: HDFC Bank is not just a great Indian bank but probably one of the best banks in the world, and through that lens it may be value-priced even though it never looks cheap on normal metrics.

ideas.idea: The 2007 Buffett lunch was 'guru dakshina' for the intellectual property that built most of his $80 million net worth, and it led to a close friendship with Charlie Munger.
ideas.detail: Buffett works to make lunch winners feel they got a bargain, gave unlimited time, and, when told Harina preferred Munger, competitively arranged a Munger lunch. Pabrai went on to play bridge with Munger and Rick Guerin every few weeks and calls Munger the smartest, most humble person he will ever meet.

ideas.idea: Dakshana exists because large inheritances are a disservice to children, leaving society as the only other place for the money.
ideas.detail: Citing Buffett's Jesse Owens analogy, a son should not start the 100-meter dash at the 40-meter line. He started Dakshana at 42 so as not to begin giving at 75 with no energy, and aims to die with $1 left.

ideas.idea: Philanthropy must be high-risk, high-return and willing to fail, because it tackles problems society has not solved, and giving money away well is harder than making it.
ideas.detail: He expected ten years of spinning wheels but Dakshana got traction within weeks. R.K. Damani of D-Mart gives about seven crores a year and Prem Watsa about $1 million a year; the model can absorb only $7-8 million annually versus $3-4 million currently spent, so the engine must grow as his compounding grows.

ideas.idea: He is always bottom-up and never starts from a sector or country; the first question is whether a business is in your circle of competence, and Covid is opportunity because trouble creates uncertainty.
ideas.detail: Jio is largely unaffected or helped by Covid while private hospitals face murky mandates and airlines were uninvestable in 2020; he quotes John Templeton that trouble is opportunity, since babies get thrown out with the bathwater.

ideas.idea: Indian Hotels is a great place to stay but he would not put a penny in at any price because of horrible capital allocation.
ideas.detail: It overpaid for the Pierre Hotel in New York after 60-65% of the best-view rooms had been sold as apartments, and guaranteed those owners free twice-daily turndown service at New York labor rates; Taj Boston was similar. Bombay House-run businesses like Corus, Tetley, TISCO and TELCO fared poorly while TCS and Titan, which it left alone, did extremely well.

ideas.idea: A Covid-hit business is only worth buying if it has great capital allocation, a balance sheet that easily survives two or three bad years, and a great core business; some businesses you should only be a customer of, never an owner.
ideas.detail: He hates hotels and airlines because price transparency means your dumbest competitor sets the price, though he respects IndiGo as the lowest-cost operator.

ideas.idea: As Munger says, why should it be easy to get rich? Be patient and act only when something is mispriced and fully understood, which may happen two or three times in two or three years.
ideas.detail: Answering a former Shree Cement CFO who never owned his own 5,000x stock, he says if an insider cannot forecast cash flows the outsider's job is harder, but you only need to be right on one such business in a 50-year investing life.

ideas.idea: Naspers' 8,000x on Tencent, from $32 million in 2001 to about $200 billion, shows that extreme patience and stepping up with a meaningful bet matter more than being right often.
ideas.detail: Naspers bought the 43% stake from Li Ka-Shing, who would be worth $230 billion instead of $30 billion had he held, and resisted pressure to sell at $1 billion, $10 billion and $100 billion. Pabrai believes Tencent is deeply undervalued even at $700 billion with too many ways to win and too few to lose, and that 'the story has just begun'.

ideas.idea: Indian unicorns will produce a few outlier winners and many disappointments, but there is no need for envy; every investment must be a no-brainer before you make it.
ideas.detail: Friends dismiss food delivery as heavy logistics with restaurants resenting 30% cuts, yet cloud kitchens and dense delivery could make the top two or three players incredible businesses in 10-20 years. You can be a very successful investor without ever making any of those bets.

ideas.idea: Run an empty calendar like Buffett and Munger: no scheduled calls, only two talks a month, emails handled in 20 minutes at 11am, then reading, naps, bridge and cycling.
ideas.detail: He sleeps late, gets a printed folder of emails at 11am and is done by 11:20, naps most afternoons, plays 5-7 hours of bridge a week, rides 20 km on weekdays and 40 km on weekends, and plays racquetball and tennis.

ideas.idea: Invert the problem: you only need one or two bets a year, so with an empty calendar you can dismiss most ideas in five minutes and go deep only on the interesting ones.
ideas.detail: Buffett and Munger used no analysts and he had none for over 20 years; he now has a couple of researchers by accident who do narrowly directed probing.

ideas.idea: Businesses in the 'death' or 'rebirth' business, funeral services, asset reconstruction, off-price retail, are really good businesses with pricing power that nobody questions.
ideas.detail: US funeral home roll-ups never go bankrupt because deaths are predictable and no one shops six funeral homes for the lowest price; TJ Maxx flourishes buying others' inventory mistakes at one-third of cost; Seritage redevelops shuttered Sears stores; Piramal buying DHFL's debt is a funeral-services business.

ideas.idea: India grows at night while the government sleeps; market-distorting regulations still shackle natural entrepreneurs, which makes him somewhat skeptical.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: India and Singapore had the same per-capita GDP 70-75 years ago and the difference now is night and day; India could grow fast for a long time if the shackles were removed, but he never picks sectors top-down.
